claim: Laetoli is a palaeontological locality in northern Tanzania.
source: Laetoli is a well-known palaeontological locality in northern Tanzania whose outstanding record includes the earliest hominin footprints in the world (3.66 million years old), discovered in 1978 at Site G and attributed to Australopithecus afarensis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction of the manuscript.

claim: The earliest hominin footprints in the world are 3.66 million years old.
source: Laetoli is a well-known palaeontological locality in northern Tanzania whose outstanding record includes the earliest hominin footprints in the world (3.66 million years old), discovered in 1978 at Site G and attributed to Australopithecus afarensis.
evidence: The age is stated in the abstract with reference to the Laetoli footprints.

claim: The earliest hominin footprints were discovered in 1978 at Site G.
source: Laetoli is a well-known palaeontological locality in northern Tanzania whose outstanding record includes the earliest hominin footprints in the world (3.66 million years old), discovered in 1978 at Site G and attributed to Australopithecus afarensis.
evidence: The discovery date and location are explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: The earliest hominin footprints are attributed to Australopithecus afarensis.
source: Laetoli is a well-known palaeontological locality in northern Tanzania whose outstanding record includes the earliest hominin footprints in the world (3.66 million years old), discovered in 1978 at Site G and attributed to Australopithecus afarensis.
evidence: The taxonomic attribution is stated in the abstract.

claim: Hominin tracks were unearthed at the new Site S at Laetoli.
source: Here, we report hominin tracks unearthed in the new Site S at Laetoli and referred to two bipedal individuals (S1 and S2) moving on the same palaeosurface and in the same direction as the three hominins documented at Site G.
evidence: The discovery of new tracks at Site S is the primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: The Site S tracks are referred to two bipedal individuals (S1 and S2).
source: Here, we report hominin tracks unearthed in the new Site S at Laetoli and referred to two bipedal individuals (S1 and S2) moving on the same palaeosurface and in the same direction as the three hominins documented at Site G.
evidence: The number of individuals and their designations are stated in the abstract.

claim: S1 and S2 were moving on the same palaeosurface as the three hominins documented at Site G.
source: Here, we report hominin tracks unearthed in the new Site S at Laetoli and referred to two bipedal individuals (S1 and S2) moving on the same palaeosurface and in the same direction as the three hominins documented at Site G.
evidence: The stratigraphic relationship is stated in the abstract and supported by geological analysis in the manuscript.

claim: S1 and S2 were moving in the same direction as the three hominins documented at Site G.
source: Here, we report hominin tracks unearthed in the new Site S at Laetoli and referred to two bipedal individuals (S1 and S2) moving on the same palaeosurface and in the same direction as the three hominins documented at Site G.
evidence: The direction of movement is stated in the abstract and supported by trackway analysis.

claim: Three hominins were documented at Site G.
source: Here, we report hominin tracks unearthed in the new Site S at Laetoli and referred to two bipedal individuals (S1 and S2) moving on the same palaeosurface and in the same direction as the three hominins documented at Site G.
evidence: The number of individuals at Site G is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The stature estimates for S1 greatly exceed those previously reconstructed for Au. afarensis from both skeletal material and footprint data.
source: The stature estimates for S1 greatly exceed those previously reconstructed for Au. afarensis from both skeletal material and footprint data.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: The evidence from Site S embodies very important additions to the Pliocene record of hominin behaviour and morphology.
source: In combination with a comparative reappraisal of the Site G footprints, the evidence collected here embodies very important additions to the Pliocene record of hominin behaviour and morphology.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement made in the abstract based on the new findings.

claim: The results are consistent with considerable body size variation within a single species of bipedal hominins as early as 3.66 million years ago.
source: Our results are consistent with considerable body size variation and, probably, degree of sexual dimorphism within a single species of bipedal hominins as early as 3.66 million years ago.
evidence: This is a major conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by stature and body mass estimates.

claim: The results are consistent with a degree of sexual dimorphism within a single species of bipedal hominins as early as 3.66 million years ago.
source: Our results are consistent with considerable body size variation and, probably, degree of sexual dimorphism within a single species of bipedal hominins as early as 3.66 million years ago.
evidence: This is a major conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by body size variation data.

claim: Estimates of body size and proportions are crucial in the evolutionary interpretation of Plio-Pleistocene hominin palaeobiology.
source: Estimates of body size and proportions are crucial in the evolutionary interpretation of Plio-Pleistocene hominin palaeobiology (McHenry, 1991, 1992; Ruff et al., 1997; Grabowski et al., 2015) and have been the subject of ongoing debates, at least since the late 1970s (e.g., Johanson and White, 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Body size and proportions have been the subject of ongoing debates since at least the late 1970s.
source: Estimates of body size and proportions are crucial in the evolutionary interpretation of Plio-Pleistocene hominin palaeobiology (McHenry, 1991, 1992; Ruff et al., 1997; Grabowski et al., 2015) and have been the subject of ongoing debates, at least since the late 1970s (e.g., Johanson and White, 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Johanson and White, 1979.

claim: Within-species variability in body size often relates to sexual dimorphism and/or to adaptation to different ecologies.
source: Within-species variability in body size often relates to sexual dimorphism and/or to adaptation to different ecologies.
evidence: This is a general statement made in the introduction based on biological principles.

claim: Extant Hominoidea show diverse patterns of variation in body size.
source: This is particularly true among extant Hominoidea, which show diverse patterns of variation (e.g., Plavcan, 2001); for instance, gorillas are polygynous species with strong sexual dimorphism due to intense male-male competition, whereas chimpanzees are promiscuous with definitively smaller sexual dimorphism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Plavcan, 2001.

claim: Gorillas are polygynous species with strong sexual dimorphism due to intense male-male competition.
source: This is particularly true among extant Hominoidea, which show diverse patterns of variation (e.g., Plavcan, 2001); for instance, gorillas are polygynous species with strong sexual dimorphism due to intense male-male competition, whereas chimpanzees are promiscuous with definitively smaller sexual dimorphism.
evidence: This is stated as an example in the introduction.

claim: Chimpanzees are promiscuous with definitively smaller sexual dimorphism.
source: This is particularly true among extant Hominoidea, which show diverse patterns of variation (e.g., Plavcan, 2001); for instance, gorillas are polygynous species with strong sexual dimorphism due to intense male-male competition, whereas chimpanzees are promiscuous with definitively smaller sexual dimorphism.
evidence: This is stated as an example in the introduction.

claim: Complex relationships among body size, sexual dimorphism, mating system and social structure/behaviour applied to extinct hominins.
source: It is reasonable to assume that complex relationships among body size, sexual dimorphism, mating system (and/or reproductive strategy) and social structure/behaviour also applied to extinct hominins, including our bipedal relatives of the Plio-Pleistocene.
evidence: This is an assumption stated in the introduction based on comparative biology.

claim: Claims that size variation in Australopithecus and/or Paranthropus was larger than that in recent human populations include inferences on sexual dimorphism.
source: In fact, claims that size variation in Australopithecus and/or Paranthropus was larger than that in recent human populations include inferences on sexual dimorphism (Richmond and Jungers, 1995; Plavcan et al., 2005; Lockwood et al., 2007; but see Reno et al., 2003), whereas arguments referring to early Homo are usually associated with eco-physiological variants (Antón et al., 2014; Di Vincenzo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Arguments referring to early Homo are usually associated with eco-physiological variants.
source: In fact, claims that size variation in Australopithecus and/or Paranthropus was larger than that in recent human populations include inferences on sexual dimorphism (Richmond and Jungers, 1995; Plavcan et al., 2005; Lockwood et al., 2007; but see Reno et al., 2003), whereas arguments referring to early Homo are usually associated with eco-physiological variants (Antón et al., 2014; Di Vincenzo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Remarkable variation in size and shape within the alleged hypodigm of Australopithecus afarensis was noted in the original description of the species.
source: For Australopithecus afarensis, remarkable variation in size and shape within its alleged hypodigm was noted in the original description of the species (Johanson et al., 1978).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Johanson et al., 1978.

claim: There have been disputes about the nature and degree of sexual dimorphism characterising Australopithecus afarensis.
source: Nevertheless, there have always been disputes about the nature and degree of sexual dimorphism characterising this early bipedal hominin, with supporters of either pronounced (e.g., Johanson and White, 1979; Kimbel and White, 1988; McHenry, 1991; Richmond and Jungers, 1995; Lockwood et al., 1996; Plavcan et al., 2005; Harmon, 2006; Gordon et al., 2008) or moderate (Lovejoy et al., 1989) body-size dimorphism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting both views.

claim: Richmond and Jungers (1995) argued that if fossils from Hadar, Maka, and Laetoli are from one sexually dimorphic species, then the degree of sexual dimorphism of Au. afarensis would have been at least as extreme as that of the most dimorphic living apes.
source: For example, Richmond and Jungers (1995) wrote: 'If the fossils from Hadar and Maka (and Laetoli) are assumed […] to be from one sexually dimorphic species, then the degree of sexual dimorphism of Au. afarensis would have been at least as extreme as that of the most dimorphic living apes […]. It follows that a strictly monogamous structure would have been highly unlikely.'
evidence: This is a direct quote from Richmond and Jungers (1995) cited in the introduction.

claim: Richmond and Jungers (1995) concluded that a strictly monogamous structure would have been highly unlikely for Au. afarensis.
source: For example, Richmond and Jungers (1995) wrote: 'If the fossils from Hadar and Maka (and Laetoli) are assumed […] to be from one sexually dimorphic species, then the degree of sexual dimorphism of Au. afarensis would have been at least as extreme as that of the most dimorphic living apes […]. It follows that a strictly monogamous structure would have been highly unlikely.'
evidence: This is a direct quote from Richmond and Jungers (1995) cited in the introduction.

claim: Reno et al. (2003) challenged the premise of extreme sexual dimorphism in Au. afarensis with an analysis of femoral head diameter.
source: Reno et al. (2003) (but see Plavcan et al., [2005] and the reply by Reno et al., [2005]) challenged this premise with an analysis of the sexual dimorphism of femoral head diameter in Au. afarensis, concluding that these early hominins showed human-like sexual dimorphism and were therefore characterised by a monogamous mating system.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Reno et al., 2003.

claim: Reno et al. (2003) concluded that Au. afarensis showed human-like sexual dimorphism and were characterised by a monogamous mating system.
source: Reno et al. (2003) (but see Plavcan et al., [2005] and the reply by Reno et al., [2005]) challenged this premise with an analysis of the sexual dimorphism of femoral head diameter in Au. afarensis, concluding that these early hominins showed human-like sexual dimorphism and were therefore characterised by a monogamous mating system.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Reno et al., 2003.

claim: Grabowski et al. (2015) obtained data supporting arguments that Au. afarensis had substantial size dimorphism leading to a large amount of variation in body size within this taxon.
source: Conversely, Grabowski et al. (2015, p. 90) obtained comprehensive and thoroughly vetted data, supporting 'arguments that Au. afarensis had substantial size dimorphism […] leading to a large amount of variation in body size within this taxon.'
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Grabowski et al., 2015.

claim: Estimates of body size and proportions of extinct creatures are largely inferred from known relationships between metric data in living species.
source: It is clear that our ability to investigate this important and controversial issue depends on the possibility of evaluating the body size and proportions of extinct creatures. Estimates are largely inferred from known relationships between metric data in living species, such as bone length (or joint size) and stature (or body mass) (McHenry, 1991, 1992; Grabowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Similar estimates can be obtained from the analysis of single footprints or trails of footprints.
source: Similar estimates can be even more plainly obtained from the analysis of single footprints or – even better – from trails of footprints (Tuttle, 1987; Dingwall et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The trackways from Laetoli Site G are ascribed to Au. afarensis.
source: Among these, one of the most remarkable pieces of evidence are the renowned trackways from Laetoli Site G (northern Tanzania), which are ascribed to Au. afarensis (White and Suwa, 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to White and Suwa, 1987.

claim: Laetoli lies within the Ngorongoro Conservation Area at the southern edge of the Serengeti Plains.
source: Laetoli (Figure 1A,B) is one of the most important palaeontological localities in Africa. It lies within the Ngorongoro Conservation Area at the southern edge of the Serengeti Plains.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The region includes sites such as Olduvai Gorge, Lake Ndutu and Laetoli itself.
source: The region includes sites such as Olduvai Gorge, Lake Ndutu and Laetoli itself and provides a long sequence of Plio-Pleistocene, mostly volcano-sedimentary, deposits that are rich in archaeological and paleontological remains (Hay, 1987), overlying Precambrian metamorphic rocks.
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with a citation.

claim: The region provides a long sequence of Plio-Pleistocene, mostly volcano-sedimentary, deposits that are rich in archaeological and paleontological remains.
source: The region includes sites such as Olduvai Gorge, Lake Ndutu and Laetoli itself and provides a long sequence of Plio-Pleistocene, mostly volcano-sedimentary, deposits that are rich in archaeological and paleontological remains (Hay, 1987), overlying Precambrian metamorphic rocks.
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with a citation to Hay, 1987.

claim: The deposits overlie Precambrian metamorphic rocks.
source: The region includes sites such as Olduvai Gorge, Lake Ndutu and Laetoli itself and provides a long sequence of Plio-Pleistocene, mostly volcano-sedimentary, deposits that are rich in archaeological and paleontological remains (Hay, 1987), overlying Precambrian metamorphic rocks.
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section.

claim: The paleoanthropological significance of the area has been known since the mid 1930s.
source: The paleoanthropological significance of the whole area has been known since the mid 1930s (Reck and Kohl-Larsen, 1936; Kohl-Larsen, 1943), whereas Laetoli became known worldwide in the 1970s for stimulating discoveries, such as the holotype and other remains of Au. afarensis (Leakey et al., 1976; Johanson et al., 1978) and remarkable evidence of the earliest bipedal hominin tracks (Leakey and Hay, 1979; Leakey and Harris, 1987) dated to 3.66 million years ago (Ma) (Deino, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with citations.

claim: Laetoli became known worldwide in the 1970s for discoveries including the holotype and other remains of Au. afarensis.
source: The paleoanthropological significance of the whole area has been known since the mid 1930s (Reck and Kohl-Larsen, 1936; Kohl-Larsen, 1943), whereas Laetoli became known worldwide in the 1970s for stimulating discoveries, such as the holotype and other remains of Au. afarensis (Leakey et al., 1976; Johanson et al., 1978) and remarkable evidence of the earliest bipedal hominin tracks (Leakey and Hay, 1979; Leakey and Harris, 1987) dated to 3.66 million years ago (Ma) (Deino, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with citations.

claim: The earliest bipedal hominin tracks at Laetoli are dated to 3.66 million years ago.
source: The paleoanthropological significance of the whole area has been known since the mid 1930s (Reck and Kohl-Larsen, 1936; Kohl-Larsen, 1943), whereas Laetoli became known worldwide in the 1970s for stimulating discoveries, such as the holotype and other remains of Au. afarensis (Leakey et al., 1976; Johanson et al., 1978) and remarkable evidence of the earliest bipedal hominin tracks (Leakey and Hay, 1979; Leakey and Harris, 1987) dated to 3.66 million years ago (Ma) (Deino, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with a citation to Deino, 2011.

claim: Mammal, bird and insect prints and trails have been identified in 18 sites out of 33 total palaeontological localities in the Laetoli area.
source: Mammal, bird and insect prints and trails have been identified in 18 sites (labelled from A to R) out of 33 total palaeontological localities in the Laetoli area (Leakey, 1987a; Musiba et al., 2008; Harrison and Kweka, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with citations.

claim: Footprints occur in 10 sublevels within the Footprint Tuff.
source: Footprints occur in 10 sublevels within the so-called Footprint Tuff, corresponding to the lower part of Tuff 7 in the Upper Laetolil Beds stratigraphic sequence (Hay, 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with a citation to Hay, 1987.

claim: The Footprint Tuff corresponds to the lower part of Tuff 7 in the Upper Laetolil Beds stratigraphic sequence.
source: Footprints occur in 10 sublevels within the so-called Footprint Tuff, corresponding to the lower part of Tuff 7 in the Upper Laetolil Beds stratigraphic sequence (Hay, 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with a citation to Hay, 1987.

claim: Hominin trackways were found in 1978 at Site G and were referred to three individuals (G1, G2, G3) of different body size.
source: These hominin trackways were found in 1978 at Site G (Locality 8) and were referred to three individuals (G1, G2, G3) of different body size: the smallest individual, G1, walked side by side on the left of the largest individual, G2, while the intermediate-sized individual, G3, superimposed its feet over those of G2 (Leakey, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with a citation to Leakey, 1981.

claim: G1 walked side by side on the left of G2.
source: These hominin trackways were found in 1978 at Site G (Locality 8) and were referred to three individuals (G1, G2, G3) of different body size: the smallest individual, G1, walked side by side on the left of the largest individual, G2, while the intermediate-sized individual, G3, superimposed its feet over those of G2 (Leakey, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with a citation to Leakey, 1981.

claim: G3 superimposed its feet over those of G2.
source: These hominin trackways were found in 1978 at Site G (Locality 8) and were referred to three individuals (G1, G2, G3) of different body size: the smallest individual, G1, walked side by side on the left of the largest individual, G2, while the intermediate-sized individual, G3, superimposed its feet over those of G2 (Leakey, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with a citation to Leakey, 1981.

claim: Au. afarensis is the only hominin taxon found to date in the Upper Laetoli Beds.
source: The trackways are usually ascribed, not without controversy (Tuttle et al., 1991; Harcourt-Smith, 2005), to Au. afarensis (White and Suwa, 1987), which is the only hominin taxon found to date in the Upper Laetoli Beds (Harrison, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the site overview section with a citation to Harrison, 2011.

claim: Site S is located about 150 m to the south of Site G.
source: The new Site S (situated within Locality 8) is located about 150 m to the south of Site G (Figure 1C), on the surface of the same morphological terrace.
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Site S is on the surface of the same morphological terrace as Site G.
source: The new Site S (situated within Locality 8) is located about 150 m to the south of Site G (Figure 1C), on the surface of the same morphological terrace.
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section.

claim: Site S was discovered during systematic survey and excavation activities aimed at evaluating the impact of a proposed new field museum at Laetoli.
source: It was discovered during systematic survey and excavation activities (Cultural Heritage Impact Assessment) aimed at evaluating the impact of a proposed new field museum at Laetoli, in the area of Locality 8.
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section.

claim: Sixty-two 2 × 2 m test pits were randomly positioned within a grid and excavated down to the Footprint Tuff.
source: Sixty-two 2 × 2 m test pits were randomly positioned within a grid and were carefully excavated down to the Footprint Tuff and sometimes deeper.
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section.

claim: In 2015, fourteen hominin tracks were unearthed in three test-pits (L8, M9 and TP2).
source: In 2015, fourteen hominin tracks always associated with tracks of other vertebrates (see Results) were unearthed in three test-pits, respectively labelled L8, M9 and TP2 from north to south (see Materials and methods) (Figures 1C and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section and shown in figures.

claim: Seven bipedal tracks were exposed in L8.
source: Seven bipedal tracks in different preservation state (see below) were exposed in L8 (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figures 3–4) and four in M9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section and shown in figures.

claim: Four bipedal tracks were exposed in M9.
source: Seven bipedal tracks in different preservation state (see below) were exposed in L8 (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figures 3–4) and four in M9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section and shown in figures.

claim: Two additional tracks of the same individual were found in the eastern part of TP2.
source: Two additional tracks of the same individual were found in the eastern part of TP2 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: All the prints in L8, M9, and TP2 are clearly referable to a single individual trackway with an estimated total length of 32 m.
source: All these prints are clearly referable to a single individual trackway, with an estimated total length of 32 m and trending SSE to NNW (i.e., 320–330°), approximately parallel to the G1 and G2/3 trackways.
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section based on analysis of the tracks.

claim: The S1 trackway trends SSE to NNW (320–330°), approximately parallel to the G1 and G2/3 trackways.
source: All these prints are clearly referable to a single individual trackway, with an estimated total length of 32 m and trending SSE to NNW (i.e., 320–330°), approximately parallel to the G1 and G2/3 trackways.
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section based on analysis of the tracks.

claim: One more track referable to a second individual (S2) was discovered in the SW corner of TP2 at the end of the September 2015 field season.
source: At the end of the September 2015 field season, we discovered one more track referable to a second individual (S2), in the SW corner of TP2.
evidence: This is stated in the discovery section.

claim: The preservation state of the tracks varies considerably along the trackway, depending on the depth of the Footprint Tuff from the surface.
source: The preservation state of the tracks varies considerably along the trackway, depending on the depth of the Footprint Tuff from the surface.
evidence: This is stated in the preservation section.

claim: In L8, the Footprint Tuff is very shallow, not deeper than 20 cm to the south.
source: In L8, the Tuff is very shallow, not deeper than 20 cm to the south, whereas it even crops out on the scarp of the terrace on the opposite side.
evidence: This is stated in the preservation section.

claim: In L8, the tracks are not filled up with compact and/or cemented sediment.
source: Consequently, the Tuff is overlain here only by reworked loose soil, and the tracks are not filled up with compact and/or cemented sediment.
evidence: This is stated in the preservation section.

claim: The first four tracks in the L8 trail are the best preserved.
source: The first four tracks in the L8 trail are the best preserved, whereas the state of preservation of the footprint-bearing surface is particularly critical in the northern part (Figure 8), where the surface appears very damaged by cracks of different size and by plant roots.
evidence: This is stated in the preservation section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Raindrop imprints are visible to the northern edge of L8.
source: Raindrop imprints are visible to the northern edge of the test-pit (Figure 2) on two relatively well-preserved portions of the tuff surrounded by weathered and lowered areas.
evidence: This is stated in the preservation section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Raindrop imprints have been described in several other footprint-bearing sites at Laetoli.
source: These features have also been described in several other footprint-bearing sites at Laetoli (Leakey, 1987a).
evidence: This is stated in the preservation section with a citation to Leakey, 1987a.

claim: In M9, about 72 cm of grey soil and unaltered sediments overlie the Footprint Tuff.
source: The situation is different in M9, where about 72 cm of grey soil and unaltered sediments overlie the Footprint Tuff.
evidence: This is stated in the preservation section.

claim: In M9, the tracks are sealed by the upper, laminated part of Tuff seven and filled with strongly cemented sediment.
source: Here, the tracks are sealed by the upper, laminated part of Tuff seven and filled with strongly cemented sediment.
evidence: This is stated in the preservation section.

claim: The infilling matrix was removed from two hominin tracks (M9/S1-2 and M9/S1-3) to examine their inner morphology.
source: In M9, the infilling matrix was removed from two hominin tracks (M9/S1-2 and M9/S1-3) (Figures 5 and 9) in order to examine their inner morphology.
evidence: This is stated in the preservation section and shown in figures.

claim: Small amounts of water were used during the excavation to soften the sediment and darken its hue.
source: Small amounts of water were used during the excavation, in order to soften the sediment and darken its hue to better distinguish it from the surrounding tuff.
evidence: This is stated in the preservation section describing excavation methods.

claim: A total of 529 footprints of mammals (excluding hominins) and birds were recorded during the September 2015 field season.
source: A total of 529 footprints of mammals (excluding hominins) and birds (Table 1) were recorded during the September 2015 field season.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1.

claim: Most of the mammal tracks can be ascribed to the genus Madoqua based on their size and morphological features.
source: Mammal tracks – mostly of small and medium-size bovids – are very abundant in M10, L8 and M9 and occur less frequently in TP2. Their size (30–40 mm long and 20–36 mm wide) and morphological features suggest that most of them can be ascribed to the genus Madoqua (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on morphological analysis.

claim: Some slightly larger prints can be referred to medium-sized bovids such as Gazella, Eudorcas or Nanger.
source: Some slightly larger prints (60–80 × 40–60 mm) can be referred to medium-sized bovids such as Gazella, Eudorcas or Nanger.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on size and morphology.

claim: It is very difficult to distinguish the footprints of Madoqua-like bovids from lagomorph footprints because of their very similar morphology and size.
source: It is very difficult to distinguish the footprints of Madoqua-like bovids from lagomorph footprints because of their very similar morphology and size (Leakey, 1987a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Leakey, 1987a.

claim: Very few prints of giraffids, equids, and rhinoceroses were identified.
source: We identified very few prints of giraffids (about 170 × 125 mm) in M10, equids (about 50–95 × 45–70 mm) in L8 and M9 and rhinoceroses (about 150–135 mm) in M9 (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in figures.

claim: Some avian prints can be referred to Galliformes of the family Numididae, such as the guinea fowl (genus Numida).
source: In M9 and M10, some avian prints (about 60 × 75 mm) often organised in trails, can be referred to Galliformes of the family Numididae, such as the guinea fowl (genus Numida) (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on morphological analysis.

claim: The assemblage of terrestrial mammal and bird footprints suggests that the local palaeoenvironment was characterised by a mosaic of dry tropical bushland, woodland, open grassland and riverine forest similar to the extant one.
source: The above-mentioned assemblage of terrestrial mammal and bird footprints suggests that the local palaeoenvironment was characterised by a mosaic of dry tropical bushland, woodland, open grassland and riverine forest similar to the extant one.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on the ichnofauna.

claim: The overall morphology of the S1 tracks matches those at Site G and is similar in particular to the prints of the larger individual, G2.
source: The overall morphology of the S1 tracks matches those at Site G (Figure 11) and is similar in particular to the prints of the larger individual, G2 (Robbins, 1987): the heel has an oval shape and is pressed deeply into the ground; the medial side of the arch is higher than the lateral one; the ball region is oriented at an angle of about 75° with respect to the longitudinal axis of the foot and is delimited anteriorly by a transversal ridge, formed when the toes gripped the wet ash and pushed it posteriorly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on morphological comparison.

claim: The heel of S1 tracks has an oval shape and is pressed deeply into the ground.
source: The overall morphology of the S1 tracks matches those at Site G (Figure 11) and is similar in particular to the prints of the larger individual, G2 (Robbins, 1987): the heel has an oval shape and is pressed deeply into the ground; the medial side of the arch is higher than the lateral one; the ball region is oriented at an angle of about 75° with respect to the longitudinal axis of the foot and is delimited anteriorly by a transversal ridge, formed when the toes gripped the wet ash and pushed it posteriorly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing track morphology.

claim: The medial side of the arch is higher than the lateral one in S1 tracks.
source: The overall morphology of the S1 tracks matches those at Site G (Figure 11) and is similar in particular to the prints of the larger individual, G2 (Robbins, 1987): the heel has an oval shape and is pressed deeply into the ground; the medial side of the arch is higher than the lateral one; the ball region is oriented at an angle of about 75° with respect to the longitudinal axis of the foot and is delimited anteriorly by a transversal ridge, formed when the toes gripped the wet ash and pushed it posteriorly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing track morphology.

claim: The ball region is oriented at an angle of about 75° with respect to the longitudinal axis of the foot in S1 tracks.
source: The overall morphology of the S1 tracks matches those at Site G (Figure 11) and is similar in particular to the prints of the larger individual, G2 (Robbins, 1987): the heel has an oval shape and is pressed deeply into the ground; the medial side of the arch is higher than the lateral one; the ball region is oriented at an angle of about 75° with respect to the longitudinal axis of the foot and is delimited anteriorly by a transversal ridge, formed when the toes gripped the wet ash and pushed it posteriorly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing track morphology.

claim: The adducted hallux extends more anteriorly than the other toes in all visible S1 footprints.
source: The adducted hallux extends more anteriorly than the other toes in all visible footprints.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing track morphology.

claim: Some S1 tracks are characterised by a posterior drag mark about 100 mm long.
source: Some tracks (especially L8/S1-3, M9/S1-2, M9/S1-3 and TP2/S1-1) are characterised by a posterior drag mark about 100 mm long (Figures 4–7 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in figures.

claim: The posterior drag marks were possibly left by the heel shuffling on the ash before being firmly placed into the soil.
source: These marks were possibly left by the heel shuffling on the ash before being firmly placed into the soil.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section.

claim: The feet were probably lifted above the ground at a low oblique angle.
source: The two latter features were also recognised in some of the G2 prints (Robbins, 1987) and suggest that the feet were probably lifted above the ground at a low oblique angle.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on track features.

claim: The weight transfer of S1 was similar to that described for G1–3.
source: The depth distribution pattern indicates that the weight transfer of S1 was similar to that described for G1–3 (Robbins, 1987): starting from the heel, the weight was transferred along the lateral part of the foot (note the steep slope of the lateral wall of the tracks compared to that on the medial side) up to the distal metatarsal region, and from here to the toes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on depth analysis.

claim: The angle of gait for S1 ranges approximately from 2° to 11°.
source: The angle of gait ranges approximately from 2° to 11°, without any particular difference between the right and left sides.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on measurements.

claim: S1 resembles G2/3 more than G1 regarding the angle of gait.
source: Regarding this aspect, S1 resembles more G2/3, for which very low average angles are reported, whereas G1 shows instead wide asymmetrical angles (Tuttle, 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Tuttle, 1987.

claim: The Laetoli hominins were all walking at similar low speed (about 0.44 to 0.9 m/s).
source: Speed estimates for S1 and G1–3 were computed starting from stride length (Figure 3) (see Materials and methods). The obtained values (Table 3) show that these hominins were all walking at similar low speed (about 0.44 to 0.9 m/s, depending on the analysis method).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on calculations shown in Table 3.

claim: The average length of the tracks in the S1 trackway is 261 mm (range 245–274).
source: The average length of the tracks in the S1 trackway is 261 mm (range 245–274).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on measurements.

claim: Lower footprint length values were measured for the three individuals at Site G compared to S1.
source: Lower values were measured for the three individuals at Site G. The average lengths are 180 mm for G1, 225 mm for G2 and 209 mm for G3 (Leakey, 1981; Tuttle, 1987) (Table 3), although a digital analysis-based study (Bennett et al., 2016) of some Site G footprint casts suggests higher values for G1 (193 mm) and G3 (228 mm).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: The main metrical features of the S1 and S2 tracks are larger than the G1–3 equivalents.
source: The main metrical features of the S1 and S2 tracks (footprint length and width, step and stride lengths) are larger than the G1–3 equivalents (Table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 3.

claim: Stature and mass estimates obtained by linear regressions from modern humans are probably exaggerations for the Laetoli track-makers.
source: It must be pointed out that stature and body-mass estimates obtained by linear regressions from modern humans (Tuttle, 1987; first method by Dingwall et al., 2013 are probably exaggerations, as the body proportions of modern Homo sapiens are considerably different from those of the Laetoli putative track-makers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological consideration.

claim: The body proportions of modern Homo sapiens are considerably different from those of the Laetoli putative track-makers.
source: It must be pointed out that stature and body-mass estimates obtained by linear regressions from modern humans (Tuttle, 1987; first method by Dingwall et al., 2013 are probably exaggerations, as the body proportions of modern Homo sapiens are considerably different from those of the Laetoli putative track-makers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological consideration.

claim: Stature estimates for S1 are about 165 cm and body mass estimates are about 44.7 kg.
source: The data in Tables 2–3 indicate that stature and mass estimates for S1 and S2 (about 165 cm and 44.7 kg, and 146 cm and 39.5 kg, respectively) are higher than those obtained for G1, G2 and G3 (with S2 partly overlapping the higher estimates for G2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on data in Tables 2-3.

claim: Stature estimates for S2 are about 146 cm and body mass estimates are about 39.5 kg.
source: The data in Tables 2–3 indicate that stature and mass estimates for S1 and S2 (about 165 cm and 44.7 kg, and 146 cm and 39.5 kg, respectively) are higher than those obtained for G1, G2 and G3 (with S2 partly overlapping the higher estimates for G2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on data in Tables 2-3.

claim: Stature and mass estimates for S1 and S2 are higher than those obtained for G1, G2 and G3.
source: The data in Tables 2–3 indicate that stature and mass estimates for S1 and S2 (about 165 cm and 44.7 kg, and 146 cm and 39.5 kg, respectively) are higher than those obtained for G1, G2 and G3 (with S2 partly overlapping the higher estimates for G2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on data in Tables 2-3.

claim: Site S is situated on an almost level or very gently dipping surface at the foot of the left (southern) side of the Garusi River valley.
source: Site S is situated on an almost level or very gently dipping surface, situated at the foot of the left (southern) side of the Garusi River valley.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the geological setting.

claim: Site G is situated about 150 m to the north of Site S, on the same surface but 1.5–2 m lower than Site S.
source: Site G is situated about 150 m to the north, on the same surface but 1.5–2 m lower than Site S.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the geological setting.

claim: There is no observable stratigraphic continuity between Sites S and G.
source: Several shallow gullies dissect this surface, producing a complexly terraced morphology: consequently, there is no observable stratigraphic continuity between the two sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the geological setting.

claim: The units in the sequence are horizontally layered and characterised by almost constant thickness.
source: However, the gullies put into light about 2–3 m of the underlying sequence, whose units are horizontally layered and characterised by almost constant thickness.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the geological setting.

claim: The Footprint Tuff can be divided into two main units – the lower and the upper one – which can be subdivided into 14 and 4 sublevels, respectively.
source: All previous literature describing the original stratigraphic setting at Laetoli (Leakey and Hay, 1979; Hay and Leakey, 1982; Hay, 1987) indicates that the Footprint Tuff can be divided into two main units – the lower and the upper one – which can be subdivided into 14 and 4 sublevels, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: Footprints occur on several sublevels of each unit of the Footprint Tuff all over the Laetoli area.
source: Footprints occur on several sublevels of each unit all over the Laetoli area: eight within the lower one (mostly on sublevel 9 and on the topmost sublevel 14), and two within the upper one (sublevels 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The hominin tracks at Site G are situated on the top of horizon B, i.e. on the top of sublevel 14 within the lower unit of the Footprint Tuff.
source: Later, Hay and Leakey (1982, p. 55 and White and Suwa (1987, p. 488 specified that the hominin tracks at Site G are situated on the top of horizon B, i.e. on the top of sublevel 14 within the lower unit of the Footprint Tuff.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The Site S tracks were printed on the uppermost level of the Finely Layered Grey and White Tuff, which corresponds to the lower subunit of the Footprint Tuff.
source: To provide a more accurate correlation within the Footprint Tuff, we observe that the Site S tracks were printed on the uppermost level of the Finely Layered Grey and White Tuff (unit 4 in the description provided in this paper), which corresponds to the lower subunit of the Footprint Tuff.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on geological analysis.

claim: No matter which method is employed to estimate stature and body mass, the two individuals S1 and S2 were taller and had a larger body mass than the G individuals.
source: Our results show that no matter which method is employed to estimate stature and body mass (see Material and methods), the two individuals S1 and S2 were taller and had a larger body mass than the G individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a key finding.

claim: The estimated about 165 cm stature of S1 is quite remarkable, exceeding G2 by more than 20 cm.
source: The estimated about 165 cm stature of S1 is quite remarkable, exceeding G2 by more than 20 cm (Table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on data in Table 3.

claim: The predicted stature of S1 exceeds any australopithecine.
source: The predicted stature of S1 exceeds any australopithecine: a mean value of 158 cm was estimated for the large Au. afarensis individual from Woranso-Mille (Haile-Selassie et al., 2010; Lovejoy et al., 2016), while the Hadar individuals range from 109 to 143 cm (McHenry, 1991; Ward et al., 2012) (Figure 12).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations and shown in Figure 12.

claim: A mean value of 158 cm was estimated for the large Au. afarensis individual from Woranso-Mille.
source: The predicted stature of S1 exceeds any australopithecine: a mean value of 158 cm was estimated for the large Au. afarensis individual from Woranso-Mille (Haile-Selassie et al., 2010; Lovejoy et al., 2016), while the Hadar individuals range from 109 to 143 cm (McHenry, 1991; Ward et al., 2012) (Figure 12).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The Hadar individuals range from 109 to 143 cm in stature.
source: The predicted stature of S1 exceeds any australopithecine: a mean value of 158 cm was estimated for the large Au. afarensis individual from Woranso-Mille (Haile-Selassie et al., 2010; Lovejoy et al., 2016), while the Hadar individuals range from 109 to 143 cm (McHenry, 1991; Ward et al., 2012) (Figure 12).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The stature of S1 falls within the range of modern Homo sapiens maximum values.
source: The stature of S1 falls within the range of modern Homo sapiens maximum values; it also fits the available Homo erectus sensu lato estimates based on fossil remains (Ruff and Walker, 1993) and on footprints (Bennett et al., 2009) (Figure 12).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations and shown in Figure 12.

claim: The stature of S1 fits the available Homo erectus sensu lato estimates based on fossil remains and on footprints.
source: The stature of S1 falls within the range of modern Homo sapiens maximum values; it also fits the available Homo erectus sensu lato estimates based on fossil remains (Ruff and Walker, 1993) and on footprints (Bennett et al., 2009) (Figure 12).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations and shown in Figure 12.

claim: The 41 to 48 kg body mass range estimated for S1 falls within the range of male Au. afarensis (40.2–61.0 kg).
source: At the same time, the 41 to 48 kg body mass range estimated for S1 (Table 3) falls easily within the range of male Au. afarensis (40.2–61.0 kg) (Grabowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Grabowski et al., 2015.

claim: S1 is identified as a large-size individual, probably a male.
source: These results extend the dimensional range of the Laetoli track-makers and identify S1 as a large-size individual, probably a male (Plavcan, 1994; Grabowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on body size estimates.

claim: The findings provide independent evidence for large body-size individuals among hominins as ancient as 3.66 Ma.
source: These findings provide independent evidence for large body-size individuals among hominins as ancient as 3.66 Ma.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a key conclusion.

claim: The body sizes of the australopithecines and of the early Homo representatives were similar.
source: Consequently, we may emphasise the conclusions by Grabowski et al. (2015) and Jungers et al. (2016), who reported that the body sizes of the australopithecines and of the early Homo representatives were similar, but also that certain australopithecine individuals (at least of Au. afarensis) were comparable with later Homo species, including H. erectus s. l. and H. sapiens.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: Certain australopithecine individuals (at least of Au. afarensis) were comparable with later Homo species, including H. erectus s. l. and H. sapiens.
source: Consequently, we may emphasise the conclusions by Grabowski et al. (2015) and Jungers et al. (2016), who reported that the body sizes of the australopithecines and of the early Homo representatives were similar, but also that certain australopithecine individuals (at least of Au. afarensis) were comparable with later Homo species, including H. erectus s. l. and H. sapiens.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The results support a nonlinear evolutionary trend in hominin body size.
source: Thus, our results support a nonlinear evolutionary trend in hominin body size (Di Vincenzo et al., 2015; Jungers et al., 2016) and contrast with the idea that the emergence of the genus Homo and/or the first dispersal out of Africa was related to an abrupt increase in body size (McHenry and Coffing, 2000; Antón et al., 2014; Maslin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The results contrast with the idea that the emergence of the genus Homo and/or the first dispersal out of Africa was related to an abrupt increase in body size.
source: Thus, our results support a nonlinear evolutionary trend in hominin body size (Di Vincenzo et al., 2015; Jungers et al., 2016) and contrast with the idea that the emergence of the genus Homo and/or the first dispersal out of Africa was related to an abrupt increase in body size (McHenry and Coffing, 2000; Antón et al., 2014; Maslin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The identification of large-size individuals among the australopithecines shows that the available fossil record can be misleading, resulting in an underestimate of the hominin phenotypic diversity in any given period.
source: The identification of large-size individuals among the australopithecines – i.e. hominins commonly presumed to be small-bodied on average – shows also that the available fossil record can be misleading, resulting in an underestimate of the hominin phenotypic diversity in any given period.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: G1 and G3 fall within the range of putative Au. afarensis females (25.5–38.1 kg) based on body-mass estimates.
source: However, the body-mass estimates suggest some observations as G1 and G3 fall within the range of putative Au. afarensis females (25.5–38.1 kg, according to Grabowski et al. [2015]), whereas G2 and S2 span across the upper female and the lower male ranges (40.2–61.0 kg, according to Grabowski et al. [2015]) .
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Grabowski et al., 2015.

claim: G2 and S2 span across the upper female and the lower male ranges (40.2–61.0 kg) based on body-mass estimates.
source: However, the body-mass estimates suggest some observations as G1 and G3 fall within the range of putative Au. afarensis females (25.5–38.1 kg, according to Grabowski et al. [2015]), whereas G2 and S2 span across the upper female and the lower male ranges (40.2–61.0 kg, according to Grabowski et al. [2015]) .
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Grabowski et al., 2015.

claim: A possible tentative conclusion is that S1 is a male; G2 and S2 are females; G1 and G3 are smaller females or juvenile individuals.
source: A possible tentative conclusion is that the various individuals represented at Laetoli are: S1, a male; G2 and S2, females; G1 and G3, smaller females or juvenile individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a tentative interpretation.

claim: Evidence for marked body-size variation in Au. afarensis based on data collected in a single site was limited until now to the fossil assemblage from the Hadar 333 locality, dated to 3.2 Ma.
source: Evidence for either marked or moderate body-size variation in Au. afarensis, based on data collected in a single site, was limited until now to the fossil assemblage from the Hadar 333 locality, dated to 3.2 Ma (with body masses ranging from 24.5 to 63.6 kg).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The new estimates for the Laetoli individuals indicate an even more marked variation in body size within the same hominin population, at 3.66 Ma.
source: The new estimates for the Laetoli individuals indicate an even more marked variation in body size within the same hominin population, at 3.66 Ma.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a key finding.

claim: The combined records from Laetoli and Hadar suggest that large-bodied hominins existed in the African Pliocene for over 400,000 years, between 3.66 and 3.2 Ma.
source: Consequently, the combined records from Laetoli and Hadar suggest that large-bodied hominins existed in the African Pliocene for over 400,000 years, between 3.66 and 3.2 Ma.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: The data contrast with the hypothesis of a temporal trend of body-size increase among Au. afarensis between the more ancient Laetoli and the more recent Hadar fossil samples.
source: At the same time, these data contrast with the hypothesis of a temporal trend of body-size increase among Au. afarensis between the more ancient Laetoli and the more recent Hadar fossil samples (Lockwood et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Lockwood et al., 2000.

claim: At least five individuals (G1, G2, G3, S1 and S2) were walking in the same time frame, in the same direction and at a similar moderate speed.
source: The impressive record of bipedal tracks from Laetoli Locality 8 (Site G and the new Site S) may open a window on the behaviour of a group of remote human ancestors, envisaging a scenario in which at least five individuals (G1, G2, G3, S1 and S2) were walking in the same time frame, in the same direction and at a similar moderate speed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the evidence.

claim: The pronounced body-size variation within the sample implies marked differences between age ranges and a considerable degree of sexual dimorphism in Au. afarensis.
source: This aspect must be evaluated in association with the pronounced body-size variation within the sample, which implies marked differences between age ranges and a considerable degree of sexual dimorphism in Au. afarensis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

claim: Reproductive strategies and social structure among at least some of the early bipedal hominins were closer to a gorilla-like model than to chimpanzees or modern humans.
source: Significant implications about the social structure of this stem hominin species derive from these physical and behavioural characteristics, suggesting that reproductive strategies and social structure among at least some of the early bipedal hominins were closer to a gorilla-like model than to chimpanzees or modern humans.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The discovery opens up the intriguing possibility that additional hominin trails may also occur in the area between Site G and Site S.
source: Finally, the discovery reported here opens up the intriguing possibility that additional hominin trails may also occur in the area between Site G and Site S.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation.

claim: The Ngorongoro Conservation Area Authority provided the permit for the fieldwork as per letter with Ref. No. NCAA/D/157/Vol. IV of June 5, 2015.
source: The Ngorongoro Conservation Area Authority (NCAA), in whose jurisdiction the site is, provided the permit for the fieldwork as per letter with Ref. No. NCAA/D/157/Vol. IV of June 5, 2015.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The foot length in H. sapiens is generally about 14% to 16% of stature.
source: Given that the foot length in H. sapiens is generally about 14% to 16% of stature (Tuttle [1987], and references therein), we computed two estimates for the Laetoli hominins assuming that their feet were, respectively, 14% and 16% of their body height (Tables 2–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation.

claim: The foot:stature ratio for Au. afarensis is 0.155–0.162.
source: This ratio is 0.155–0.162 (Dingwall et al., 2013), so we obtained stature estimates (Tables 2–3) predictably close to or slightly lower than the lower limit of the estimates given by the Tuttle (1987) method.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation to Dingwall et al., 2013.

claim: The transitional speed from walk to run is around 2.2 m/s.
source: The transitional speed from walk to run is around 2.2 m/s (Dingwall et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation to Dingwall et al., 2013.
